title: COPs and Climate Finance

cards.h: COP outcomes are the most current part of the paper
cards.b:
UPSC asks about the latest COP, the finance goal and India’s position. These answers must carry names, numbers and years.

As of 2026: COP30 (Belém, Brazil) ended in November 2025. COP31 is due in Antalya, Türkiye in November 2026 as this lesson is written, so check its outcome.

The Conference of the Parties is the supreme body of the UNFCCC. It meets every year. A Presidency (host country) steers talks, and decisions are by consensus. The Subsidiary Bodies (SBSTA, SBI) prepare technical work.

Alongside it, the CMA governs the Paris Agreement.

COP28 (Dubai): the first Global Stocktake called for transitioning away from fossil fuels, tripling renewable capacity to 11,000 GW and doubling efficiency by 2030. The Loss and Damage Fund was launched on day one.

COP29 (Baku): the New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) set $300 billion a year by 2035 from developed countries, within a wider aim of $1.3 trillion a year from all sources. India called the offer inadequate. Article 6 carbon market rules were also settled.

COP30 was held in Belém, Brazil, in the Amazon. It ended with the Global Mutirão decision. Main results: a call to triple adaptation finance by 2035 (without a clear base year), voluntary Belém adaptation indicators, a Just Transition mechanism, a two-year work programme on climate finance and a push to speed up implementation.

The text did not name a roadmap to end fossil fuels, and deforestation had no roadmap in the final text. Brazil promised to prepare voluntary roadmaps. The Tropical Forests Forever Facility was launched with pledges from some countries.

India stressed equity, CBDR-RC and finance, and opposed unilateral trade measures like the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), whose definitive phase began in January 2026. It supported adaptation finance and a just transition.

India argued that developed countries must deliver the earlier $100 billion promise and scale it up before asking developing countries to do more.

Türkiye will host COP31 in Antalya in November 2026. Under a compromise, Australia leads the negotiations as President of the negotiations, and a pre-COP in the Pacific is planned (as of 2026, reports; verify final arrangements).

Watch for the 2035 NDC gap, the finance work programme, adaptation indicators and the fossil fuel roadmap.

• Global Environment Facility (1991): finances UNFCCC, CBD and UNCCD work.
  • Green Climate Fund (Cancun 2010, Songdo, South Korea): the largest dedicated fund.
  • Adaptation Fund (under Kyoto).
  • Loss and Damage Fund (operational from COP28; hosted by the World Bank).
  • LDCF and SCCF for least developed countries.

Copenhagen (2009) promised $100 billion a year by 2020. The OECD reported it was first met in 2022. Developing countries dispute how loans are counted and how much is grant.

The NCQG replaces it from 2025, but the $300 billion figure is far below the $1.3 trillion need, and much will be loans.

Most money goes to mitigation, such as solar. Adaptation gets less and loss and damage the least. Climate finance is also seen as debt creation for poor countries.

Rich countries say public money is limited and private capital must be mobilised. Developing countries want public grants.

Mains-style: “Climate finance is the real test of Paris. Examine the gaps and India’s position.” Structure: needs; promise ($100 billion, NCQG $300 billion); gaps (loans, accounting, adaptation); India’s demand (grants, CBDR, no CBAM); way forward (reform of MDBs, Article 6, carbon markets).

Prelims tip: GCF from Cancun 2010, HQ in Songdo. NCQG is $300 billion by 2035. COP28 Dubai started the Loss and Damage Fund.
